parole.significato: A rope of hair or maguey fibre, for tying horses, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mecate, from a Nahuan language; cf. Classical Nahuatl mecatl.

parole.significato: A crescent-shaped corral used in Chilean rodeos.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish medialuna (literally “half moon”).

parole.significato: A Caribbean sandwich of roast pork, ham, mustard, Swiss cheese, and dill pickles.
parole.testo: From Spanish medianoche (“midnight”), since it was served in nightclubs.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of dry measure, equivalent to about 2.3 L.
parole.testo: From Spanish medio (“half, half-celemin, half-real, etc.”), from Latin medius (“half”), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Doublet of medium, media, and mediate.

parole.significato: A bonito or greater amberjack (Seriola fasciata).
parole.testo: From Spanish medregal.

parole.significato: a mixture of sugar and molasses; crude sugar as it comes from the pans without being drained
parole.testo: From Spanish melado, from melar (“to sugar, to candy”).

parole.significato: A kind of yellow-fleshed peach having red skin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish melocotón (“peach tree and its fruit”), from Latin mālum cotōnium (“quince, or quince tree”, literally “apple of Cydonia”).

parole.significato: A beggar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mendigo.

parole.significato: A traditional Mexican soup made with tripe and chili peppers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish menudo. Doublet of minute and menu.

parole.significato: A minimarket in Latin America.
parole.testo: From Spanish mercadito.

parole.significato: A type of music common in the Caribbean, originally associated with the Dominican Republic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish merengue, from French meringue. Doublet of meringue.

parole.significato: A sheep of a Spanish breed with long, fine hair.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish merino.

parole.significato: Any of several large groupers of warm seas.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mero.

parole.significato: A flat area of land or plateau higher than other land, with one or more clifflike edges.
parole.testo: First attested 1759, from Spanish mesa (“table”), from Latin mēnsa. Doublet of mensa.

parole.significato: A plateau, especially in Spanish-speaking countries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish meseta.

parole.significato: Any of several deciduous trees of the genus Prosopis found in America, and used as forage, which have long, beige seed…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mezquite, mizquite, from Nahuatl mizquitl (“the mesquite tree”).

parole.significato: A genre of Spanish music that features a blend of contemporary and classical sounds
parole.testo: From Spanish mestizo. Doublet of mestizo.

parole.significato: The postrevolutionary construction of a modern Mexican national identity.
parole.testo: From Spanish mestizaje.

parole.significato: A person of mixed ancestry, especially one of Spanish and Native American heritage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mestizo, from Late Latin mixtīcius, from Latin mixtus (“mixed”). Doublet of metis, which came from French.

parole.significato: A flat stone with a slightly concave surface, used with another stone (a mano) for grinding maize or other grains.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish metate, from a Nahuan language, from Proto-Nahuan *mətla-tl.

parole.significato: A member of an indigenous people of the Americas
parole.testo: From Spanish mexica, from Classical Nahuatl mēxihcah, absolutive plural form of mēxihcatl (“Mexica, Aztec”).

parole.significato: A Mexica; an Aztec.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mexicano, from Nahuatl mēxihcah plural of mēxihcatl (“a Mexica”) + -ano (“-an”). By surface analysis, Mexico + -an. Doublet of Mexicano.

parole.significato: A store that sells Mexican products.
parole.testo: From Spanish mexicana.

parole.significato: A Mexican (especially male).
parole.testo: From Spanish mexicano. Doublet of Mexican.

parole.significato: A person who distills mezcal.
parole.testo: From Spanish mezcalero.

parole.significato: A Moorish or Spanish mosque.
parole.testo: From Spanish mezquita. Doublet of mosque.

parole.significato: What is mine is yours; a friendly expression of sharing.
parole.testo: From the Spanish mi casa es su casa (“make yourself at home”, literally “my house is your house”).

parole.significato: A small South American monkey (Mico melanurus, syn. Callithrix melanura), allied to the marmoset.
parole.testo: From Spanish or Portuguese mico.

parole.significato: shit
parole.testo: Directly from Spanish mierda, from Latin merda. Doublet of merde and merd.

parole.significato: A term of endearment for a woman or girl.
parole.testo: From Spanish mija.

parole.significato: A term of endearment for a man or boy; dear, darling, my heart.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mijo.

parole.significato: A traditional religious folk charm of Latin America and nearby regions, coming in a variety of forms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish milagro (“miracle”), from Latin mīrāculum. Doublet of miracle and miraculum.

parole.significato: A thin slice of beef or another meat, dipped into beaten eggs, seasoned with salt and other condiments (like parsley an…
parole.testo: From Spanish milanesa.

parole.significato: Spanish mile, a traditional Spanish unit of distance equivalent to about 1.4 km.
parole.testo: From Spanish milla (“Spanish mile”), from Latin mīlia (“Roman mile”), plural of mīlle (“1000”) in reference to its composition of 1000 Roman paces. Doublet of mile and milha.

parole.significato: A form of music originating in Argentina, Uruguay, and Southern Brazil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish milonga, in turn from Brazilian Portuguese milonga (“chant”). Theories connect the word to the nineteenth century slave trade between South America and Africa. parole.significato: Someone who performs milonga music, especially as a singer.
parole.testo: Spanish

parole.significato: A cyclical crop-growing system used throughout Mesoamerica.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish milpa, from Classical Nahuatl.

parole.significato: A tower that offers a panoramic view.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mirador.

parole.significato: A variety of chili; when dried, the chilis are called guajillos.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mirasol (“sunflower”)

parole.significato: Pertaining to a Native American people living in the region of Moskitia in Central America.
parole.testo: From Spanish Mosquito, and its source, Miskito Miskito, of unknown origin.

parole.significato: A kind of small sailing vessel historically used in the Mediterranean, rigged partly like a xebec and partly like a fel…
parole.testo: From Spanish místico. Compare Catalan místic, French mistique, Italian mistico, and Ottoman Turkish مستقو (mistiko). These all refer to sailing ships of the Mediterranean, but not necessarily to the same kind of ship. The number of masts is variously two or three and the sails are lateen or square.

parole.significato: A final campaign rally done by candidates of one political party usually the night before an election.
parole.testo: From Spanish mitin de avance (literally “rally of progress; rally of advance”), from mitin + de + avance, where mitin itself is from English meeting. Compare Tagalog miting de abanse.

parole.significato: A member of a Mesoamerican people who live primarily in southern Mexico.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mixteco, alteration of mixteca, from Classical Nahuatl mixtēcah (“Mixtecs”, plural).

parole.significato: A large leather covering for the saddle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mochila. Doublet of macheer.

parole.significato: A modernist, especially a militantly devoted supporter of modernism
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish modernista.

parole.significato: A Caribbean dish of fried green plantains or yuca seasoned with garlic, olive oil and pork crackling, then mashed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mofongo.

parole.significato: A member of a pre-Columbian culture that existed from 300 CE to 1300 CE in the desert of present day Arizona.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish Mogollón. The culture's name derives from the Mogollon Mountains, in which they lived, which in turn were named after Juan Ignacio Flores Mogollon. The surname is mostly found in Venezuela.

parole.significato: A generally isolated, steep-sided residual hill, composed of limestone, marble, or dolomite and surrounded by nearly fl…
parole.testo: From Spanish mogote.

parole.significato: wetback
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mojado (literally “wet”), from espalda mojada.

parole.significato: A Mediterranean dish consisting of filleted salt-cured tuna.
parole.testo: From Spanish mojama, from Arabic مُشَمَّع (mušammaʕ, “of wax”).

parole.significato: A Cuban cocktail, generally made from rum, lime, sugar, mint, etc.
parole.testo: From Spanish mojito, diminutive of mojo (“sauce”), from mojar (“to moisten”), from Vulgar Latin *molliō (“to soften by soaking”), from Latin molliō (“soften”), from mollis (“soft”).

parole.significato: Any of various sauces originating in the Canary Islands and made with olive oil, peppers, garlic, paprika, and other sp…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mojo.

parole.significato: A tree, either Vitex parviflora or Vitex cofassus in the family Lamiaceae.
parole.testo: From Spanish molave, from Tagalog mulawin.

parole.significato: A traditional Mexican stone tool, equivalent in function to a mortar and pestle, used for grinding food.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish molcajete, from Classical Nahuatl mōlcaxitl.

parole.significato: Any of several spicy sauces typical of the cuisine of Mexico and neighboring Central America countries, especially one…
parole.testo: From Spanish mole, from Classical Nahuatl mōlli (“sauce; stew; something ground”).

parole.significato: A traditional Mexican wood whisk that is twirled between the palms in order to stir hot beverages such as hot chocolate…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish molinillo.

parole.significato: A deciding instant; the time when a test determines or makes it apparent whether something will succeed.
parole.testo: A calque of Spanish momento de la verdad, which refers to the time of the final sword thrust in a bullfight.

parole.significato: Cercopithecus mona, a West African monkey.
parole.testo: From Spanish mona (“monkey”).

parole.significato: A Latin American soup made from tripe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mondongo (“tripe”).

parole.significato: A mung bean.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mongo . Compare Tagalog munggo. Doublet of mung.

parole.significato: Any of the genus Dromiciops of small marsupials, in the order Microbiotheria, native to Chile and Argentina.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish monito del monte (“little monkey of the bush”).

parole.significato: Any of several birds in the genus Xolmis in the tyrant flycatcher family.
parole.testo: From Spanish monjita (“little nun”).

parole.significato: A picador's assistant
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish monosabio.

parole.significato: A type of longsword used in the 16th and 17th centuries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish montante or a cognate in another language.

parole.significato: A game in which three or four cards are dealt face-up and players bet on which of them will first be matched in suit by…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish monte (“mountain”): in the sense of the card game, referring to the stack of unplayed cards. Doublet of mount.

parole.significato: A traditional Iberian hat associated with bullfighters.
parole.testo: From Spanish.

parole.significato: Of a style reminiscent of the architecture of Alta California.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish Monterrey, from Galician Monterrei, from monte (“mountain”) + rei (“king”).

parole.significato: A round Spanish cap, with flaps at the back or sides, once used by hunters.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish montero (“huntsman”).

parole.significato: A heap of ore; a mass undergoing the process of amalgamation.
parole.testo: From Spanish montón (“head”).

parole.significato: The counterpoint in Cuban salsa music.
parole.testo: From Spanish montuno (literally “from the mountain”), referring to rural music.

parole.significato: a religious meeting hall associated with the Penitente Brotherhood of New Mexico
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish morada.

parole.significato: A Spanish blood sausage, sometimes with rice and onions as ingredients.
parole.testo: From Spanish morcilla.

parole.significato: A Moor, especially one who had converted to Christianity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish morisco (“Moorish”), from moro (“Moor”).

parole.significato: A Muslim inhabitant of the Philippines
parole.testo: From Spanish moro (“Moor”). Doublet of Moor.

parole.significato: A twenty-dollar coin of Venezuela.
parole.testo: From Spanish morocota.

parole.significato: A Central American sausage made from pigs' blood.
parole.testo: From Spanish moronga.

parole.significato: A dish of black beans and white riced cooked together; congri.
parole.testo: From its Spanish name, Spanish moros y cristianos (literally “Moors and Christians”), in reference to the colors of the two ingredients.

parole.significato: A round hill or point of land.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish morro.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mosquito (“gnat”), diminutive of mosca (“fly”), from Latin musca (“fly”), from Proto-Indo-European *mūs- (“fly, stinging fly, gnat”). Cognate with West Flemish meuzie (“mosquito”), dialectal Swedish mausa (“fly”), Lithuanian musė (“a fly”) and Sicilian muschitta (“midge”). See

parole.significato: A large or rich vein of gold or of another precious mineral from which other branches extend.
parole.testo: Probably a calque of Spanish veta madre (“mother lode”).

parole.significato: The driver of a mototaxi.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mototaxista and Portuguese mototaxista.

parole.significato: An Iberian Christian living under Arab domination.
parole.testo: From Spanish mozárabe, from Arabic مُسْتَعْرِب (mustaʕrib).

parole.significato: A male servant, especially an attendant to a bullfighter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mozo.

parole.significato: Thanks!
parole.testo: A jocular malapropism of Spanish muchas gracias.

parole.significato: A Latino woman or girl.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish muchacha.

parole.significato: An informal term of address, especially to a young man; similar to man, chap, dude, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish muchacho.

parole.significato: Much; a great deal of.
parole.testo: From Spanish mucho. Unrelated to much.

parole.significato: Thank you very much.
parole.testo: Spanish muchas gracias (“many thanks”) but with muchos in the more familiar (and grammatically incorrect) masculine form.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Moors of al-Andalus who remained in Christian territory after the Reconquista but were not conv…
parole.testo: From Spanish mudéjar, from Arabic مُدَجَّن (mudajjan, “domesticated”), from the verb دَجَّنَ (dajjana, “to tame”), from دَجَنَ (dajana, “to become accustomed”).

parole.significato: Eucryphia cordifolia, a South American tree.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish muermo.

parole.significato: Among Puebloan peoples, a man who was notionally transformed into a woman and took the passive role in the sexual relat…
parole.testo: From Spanish mujerado, see mujer (“woman”), -ado (“-ated, -ified”).

parole.significato: A drove of mules.
parole.testo: From Spanish mulada.

parole.significato: a chili pepper (Capsicum annuum), related to the poblano and usually sold dried.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mulato. Doublet of mulatto.

parole.significato: A red flag used by bullfighters.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish muleta, diminutive of mula (“mule”).

parole.significato: Dasypus hybridus, the southern long-nosed armadillo.
parole.testo: From Spanish mulita.

parole.significato: Offal; waste animal product; organic matter unfit for consumption.
parole.testo: From the Spanish mondongo (“tripe, entrails”), perhaps via its English etymon mondongo.

parole.significato: A municipality in various Latin American countries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish municipio. Doublet of municipium.

parole.significato: An unrefined brown sugar with a strong flavour of molasses.
parole.testo: Corrupted from Spanish mascabado or Portuguese mascavado, from the verb mascavar, a corrupted form of menoscabar (“to despise”).

parole.significato: A child who is 1/16 black: the offspring of a mustee and a white parent.
parole.testo: From Spanish mestizo fino or a short form thereof; compare English mustee from Spanish mestizo.

parole.significato: Very.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish muy.

parole.significato: A genre of Chilean music emphasising sentimentality and intimacy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish música cebolla.

parole.significato: Nothing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish nada (“nothing”). Doublet of natal, Natal, née, and Noel.

parole.significato: An animal form which a person may take.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish nahual, from Classical Nahuatl nāhualli (“sorcerer, spirit, animal form a person may take”).

parole.significato: A member of a group of people indigenous to Central Mexico, spanning multiple tribal groups and including the Aztecs.
parole.testo: From Spanish náhuatl, from Classical Nahuatl nahuatl, nahuatlatolli (“the clear or understandable language”).

parole.significato: An interpreter in an indigenous language, not necessarily Nahuatl.
parole.testo: From Spanish nahuatlato, from Nahuatl nāhuatlahtoh.

parole.significato: Synonym of Nahuatlism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish nahuatlismo.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Nambé people or the variety of Tewa they speak.
parole.testo: From Spanish Nambé, from Tewa Nąnbeʼ (“rounded earth”).

parole.significato: Any of several types of true yam (Dioscorea) used in Caribbean Spanish cooking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish ñame, substituting n for the unfamiliar Spanish letter ñ. Doublet of yam.

parole.significato: To run away; to leave; to depart.
parole.testo: UK 19th century. Probably from Spanish vamos (“we go”) or vámonos (“let's go”). Possibly influenced by German nehmen (“to take”). Cognate with English vamoose. Possibly backslang from summon.

parole.significato: A large shrub or small tree of subtropical and tropical areas of the Americas, Byrsonima crassifolia, bearing a small,…
parole.testo: From American Spanish nance, from Classical Nahuatl.

parole.significato: A Spanish or Portuguese carrack.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish nao.

parole.significato: A perfume distilled from the orange blossom.
parole.testo: From Spanish nafa.

parole.significato: Solanum quitoense, a subtropical perennial plant from northwestern South America.
parole.testo: From Spanish naranjilla.

parole.significato: A genre of Mexican music based on the polka, depicting drug smugglers, cartels, and other criminal activities.
parole.testo: From Spanish narcocorrido, from narco- (“drug”) + corrido (“ballad”).

parole.significato: narcodollar
parole.testo: From Spanish narcodólar, from English narcodollar.

parole.significato: The sapodilla tree.
parole.testo: From Spanish níspero, influenced by berry.

parole.significato: A chewy, translucent jelly produced by the fermentation of coconut water, a delicacy of the Philippines.
parole.testo: From Spanish nata de coco (literally “coconut cream”).

parole.significato: A member of the Navajo people, currently the largest Native American tribe in North America.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish navajo, from Tewa navahúuˀu (“field adjoining an arroyo”).

parole.significato: hard razor clam (Tagelus dombeii)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish navajuela, diminutive of navaja (“razor clam”)

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the Philippine island of Negros
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish negrense.

parole.significato: An African Pygmy.
parole.testo: From Spanish negrillo, from negro + -illo.

parole.significato: Left over water after nixtamalization.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish nejayote, from a Nahuan language; cf. Guerrero Nahuatl nexayotl, Tlamacazapa Nahuatl nexayotl, Pipil nexāyut.

parole.significato: A type of Moorish Revival architecture popular in the Iberian Peninsula in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish neomudéjar or neo- + Mudéjar.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Neocatechumenal Way, a community-based Catholic movement founded in Madrid in 1964.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish Neocatecumenal, equivalent to neo- + catechumenal.

parole.significato: Experimental reggaeton.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Spanish neoperreo.

parole.significato: Of or relating to natives or inhabitants of the mainland United States (especially New York) who are of Puerto Rican de…
parole.testo: From neo- + (Puerto) Rican, modeled after Spanish neorriqueño, itself a blend of neoyorquino (“New Yorker”) + puertorriqueño (“Puerto Rican”).

parole.significato: Nicaraguan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish nica.

parole.significato: A tropical flea, the chigoe.
parole.testo: From Spanish nigua, from Taíno [Term?].

parole.significato: The loquat, Eriobotrya japonica.
parole.testo: From Spanish níspero (“medlar, loquat”), from Latin mespilum (“medlar”).

parole.significato: Not good; no good; bad.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Hispanism, derived from no + bueno, a calque of no good. The closest equivalent to the adjective in Spanish is no estar bien (literally, “to not be good”); however it is a phrase rather than an adjective.

parole.significato: I do not like (this).
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Spanish no me gusta.

parole.significato: no more
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish no más (“only, just”). Its use as an interjection is a pseudo-Hispanism derived from an English-to-Spanish calque of no more.

parole.significato: A person with Hispanic heritage who grew up in a non-Spanish speaking country and knows little to no Spanish.
parole.testo: From Spanish (yo) no sabo, an incorrect way of saying no sé (“I don't know”), + kid.

parole.significato: A sauce made from walnuts and spices.
parole.testo: From Spanish nogada.

parole.significato: A prickly pear cactus from the genus Opuntia, especially Opuntia cochinellifera; the edible pads (fleshy leaves) of the…
parole.testo: From Spanish nopal, from Classical Nahuatl nohpalli (“Opuntia cactus”). Compare nopales.

parole.significato: The leaves of a prickly pear cactus, as used in Mexican cooking.
parole.testo: From Spanish nopales, plural of nopal.

parole.significato: A treadwheel with attached buckets, used to raise and deposit water.
parole.testo: From Spanish noria, from Arabic نَاعُورَة (nāʕūra), from Classical Syriac ܢܥܘܪܬܐ (nāʿōrtāʾ, “water wheel; growler”), from ܢܥܪ (nʿar, “to roar, growl, bray”).

parole.significato: A song in the norteño genre.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Spanish norteña.

parole.significato: A Mexican gang.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish norteño (“northerner”), from the gang's territory in Northern California.

parole.significato: A genre of Mexican music related to polka and corridos, emerged in the late 19th century.
parole.testo: From Spanish norteño (“Northern [Mexico]”).

parole.significato: A bullfight between a novillo and a novillero.
parole.testo: From Spanish novillada.

parole.significato: A young trainee bullfighter (who fights against novillos).
parole.testo: From Spanish novillero.

parole.significato: A young bull (fought by a novillero).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish novillo.

parole.significato: New or novel, usually in reference to Latin American culture.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish nuevo. Doublet of new.

parole.significato: The ecclesiastic title of a permanent diplomatic representative of the Roman Catholic Church to a sovereign state or in…
parole.testo: From Spanish nuncio, from Latin nūntius (“envoy”).

parole.significato: The coypu, Myocastor coypus.
parole.testo: From Spanish nutria (“otter”), from Latin lutra.

parole.significato: Or something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish o algo así. Amerimutt memes often ended sentences in or something to mock Americans for their overuse of the phrase. This was then translated to Spanish to mock Mexicans in the Meximutt meme.

parole.significato: A semihard white cheese from the Oaxaca region of Mexico.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish Oaxaca, from Classical Nahuatl Huāxyacac, from Huāxacatzin (“name of a hill”), from huāxin (huaje) (Leucaena leucocephala) + yacatl (“nose”) + -tzin (“honorific suffix”).

parole.significato: A dessert from several countries in Latin America, consisting of two thin wafers sandwiching a sweet filling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish oblea.

parole.significato: Any member of the species Oxalis tuberosa (syn. Oxalis crenata), which bear edible tubers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish oca, from Quechua uqa.

parole.significato: A traditional Spanish unit of mass, equivalent to about 3.6 g.
parole.testo: From Spanish ochava (“⅛ Spanish ounce”), from Latin octāvus (“one-eighth”). Doublet of octave, octavo, and oitava.

parole.significato: A former Spanish coin from the 17th to 19th centuries.
parole.testo: Spanish ochavo

parole.significato: Any of various pine trees of Latin America.
parole.testo: Spanish ocote

parole.significato: Any of various succulent plants, not closely related to the cactus, in genus Fouquieria, especially Fouquieria splenden…
parole.testo: From American Spanish ocotillo, from ocote.

parole.significato: Someone having one-eighth black ancestry.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish octorón; compare quadroon from cuarterón (“quadroon”).

parole.significato: Occupied (said of a toilet stall).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish ocupado.

parole.significato: Expressing approval or encouragement.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish tilde, from Latin titulus (“superscript”) or from tildar. Doublet of titer/titre, title, titlo, tittle, and titulus. Compare Portuguese til.

parole.significato: A sidekick.
parole.testo: From Spanish tonto (“fool, idiot”), the Spanish name for the tribe, a calque of Western Apache kounʼnde (“wild rough people”). The fictional character (described as Comanche or Potawatomi) either from Potawatomi [Term?] or named after Tonto Basin, Arizona.

parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τράγος (trágos, “goat”) + -ism. Alternatively, OED indicates an adaptation from Spanish tragalismo, of the same Ancient Greek origin.

parole.testo: From Swedish trona or from Spanish trona, both derived from Arabic أَطْرُون (ʔaṭrūn), from نَطْرُون (naṭrūn), from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron), ultimately from Egyptian nṯrj: R9. Doublet of natron and niter.

parole.significato: = The ultimum; the final, ultimate point of a sequence.
parole.testo: First attested in 1622; from either the Italian ultimo, or the Portuguese último, or the Spanish ultimo; compare ultime.
